catalog_citation: Crowley, Terry. 2002. Gela. In John Lynch, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley (eds), The Oceanic Languages, 525-537. Richmond: Curzon. (archive.org djvu scanned text, local cache)
catalog_quote: 1.3 Stress Stress is applied to the penultimate syllable of the word. With the addition of morphological material after a root, the penultimate syllable of the actual root may be unstressed. When two identical vowels arise word-finally with an intervening morpheme boundary, the resulting sequence is pronounced as a single stressed vowel. Thus compare /'tolu/ ‘three’ with /kolu-u/ ‘with me’ > /ko'lu/.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable; all syllables are open (CV), so weight plays no role. One sentence only; no examples, no mention of secondary stress or exceptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Ivens 1937 describes 'Florida' = the language of the two larger islands called Nggela (Nggela Sule and Nggela Pile), based on Melanesian Mission translations rather than fieldwork; he says the Olevuga (western island) variety 'does not differ materially' (p. 1075). This is the Gela of the catalog.

new_statements.quote: In Nggela the accent is always on the penultimate syllable so that the addition of a suffix throws the accent forward; bósa, bosáva (speech); mána, manáha. [p. 142] -- When these short forms are used as the object they must be considered as suffixes since the accent is altered: rígi, see; rigíu, rigígo, rigía, but as subject these forms are written separate: u rigia. [p. 150] -- Ga makes abstract nouns from verbs and adjectives. Since it is suffixed the accent is thrown forward: ndólo, to love, ndológa, love [p. 153]

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record for Gela is penultimate stress = fixed penultimate; Fox states penultimate accent explicitly and adds the detail that suffixes (including enclitic object pronouns) fall inside the stress domain while the demonstrative ka does not. Also matches Ivens 1937 p. 1077 ('The stress is on the penultimate syllable') already recorded in this language's. How opened: live host www.jps.auckland.ac.nz reset every TCP connection again (browser User-Agent, https home page and http document URL); the the Internet Archive CDX index located capture 20120907014417 of the JPS full-text HTML page (whole article inline, page breaks marked '- NNN'), downloaded by automated download and. no scanned n…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the penultimate syllable without exception; suffixes (transitive -vi/-va, nominalising -ga, -ha, suffixed short object pronouns -u/-go/-a) count in the stress domain, so accent shifts rightward to stay penultimate (bósa > bosáva, rígi > rigía, ndólo > ndológa). Postposed demonstrative ka does not shift the accent and is therefore written as a separate word (p. 154).
new_statements.exceptions: None; Fox says 'always'. He uses accent placement as a diagnostic for suffix vs. separate particle (object pronouns are suffixes because they shift accent; demonstrative ka is separate because it does not).
new_statements.identity_note: Fox writes 'Nggela' for the language of Florida Island (Nggela Sule / Nggela Pile), the same language as catalog 'Gela' (gela1263); he notes Codrington and Ivens call it 'Florida' and Patteson/Gabelentz 'Anudha'. No particular dialect is singled out for the accent statement.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in both held Crowley 2002 excerpts at section 1.3, p.526. Deciding source is a 2002 linguist-authored grammar sketch (Curzon Oceanic Languages volume) with an explicit stress section — short, single-consultant, but the most recent professional description; Codrington 1885 p.523 (downloaded now to independently gives penultimate accent for Florida/Gela, so two sources 117 years apart agree and nothing suggests the penultimate coding is wrong. The one work that could deepen the record is Miller 1975 (609 pp SOAS PhD, syntax-focused, stress coverage unverified, could not be reached by automated download).

sources.quote: The syllable structure in Gela is C(V). Word stress generally occurs on each word’s penultimate syllable, but the addition of morphemes after the root may cause the penultimate syllable to become unstressed (Crowley 2002). Preliminary studies have shown that a stressed syllable has higher F0 and intensity, and longer duration than its unstressed counterpart.
